subject: overlap with small sample size/short durations

messages.author: 0a784edb642f758b
messages.subject: overlap with small sample size/short durations
parts:
Hello! Hope all is well. I’m working on a quantitative spatial analysis of two somewhat cryptic species of marine mammals (Zc and Md). One factor that I’d like to look into is the area used/home ranges. Most of my questions are more theoretical as opposed to specific in relation to the package. 

We have ARGOS tag data for several resident individuals, ranging from 14 days to 158 (mean=39, med=34). One species’ (Zc) deployment times are overall shorter than the others (Md). When I run the variograms, only a handful of the individuals with durations over twenty days indicate any potential home range residency captured by the tags. 

Here are the variograms for each individual. The best fit model for the majority here was determined to be OUF anisotropic. 


Using the acceptable variograms, I came up with some overlap shapefiles of the CIs using the overlap function using both sets. However, due to the small number of individuals, the overlap and CIs are far too wide and confusing, often incorporating areas that only two individuals briefly visited due to the small sample sizes. 

In hopes of having more individuals with acceptable variograms, and taking advice from another post here, I cut some of the longer durations into parts based on the individual’s location and when it shifted habitat/area/region. That provided several new variograms for previously unacceptable variograms (below), mostly again fit to the OUF anisotropic model. I kept each new track to a minimum of 19 days (obviously a very short duration). Basically, I'm curious if this is an acceptable practice for this method of kernel density estimation. Still, it provides strange overlap estimates for the Zc species(shown at the bottom and not yet excluding land). 


I mostly am curious if you have advice for narrowing down the overlap with such a small sample size and why it has been split up like this. Thank you so much! I can provide any further information necessary.

Zc overlap estimtate with split proper variograms

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: overlap with small sample size/short durations
parts:
Hi Danny,

From looking at your variograms, it appears that your effective sample sizes are going to be very small, which means that your area estimates and overlap estimates will be very uncertain. There are some guidelines for effective sample sizes give in: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
If the non-resident looking variograms do correspond to range shifts, then it is good to segment that data to address home-range estimation, though keeping in mind that there is more space use over longer periods of time.

Aside from that, what do you mean by the overlap estimates being strange? Do the point estimates not roughly correspond to what you see in the two distributions?

Best,
Chris

Chis,

Sorry, I have a few further questions if you don't mind!

It is my inclination that ZcTag044 is not stable after Lag(day) 20 or so, with at least ZcTag018 also featuring some range shifts towards the end of their variograms. All of these were fit to OUF models. None of these seem to feature very asymptotic behavior, which of course may be a symptom of their short lengths. These have been calculated using the pHREML method to reduce bias and I'm in the process of getting started potentially incorporating parametric bootstrapping.  Do you have any suggestions for incorporating variograms like these other than dividing them where shifts seem to occur? Since this is ARGOS data, would it be necessary to incorporate error somehow? These are all resident individuals with large ranges.

Danny

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: overlap with small sample size/short durations
parts:
Hi Danny,

ZcTag044 does appear to be stable for about 20 day, and if the theoretical variogram of the fitted model runs through that trend, then that would be a success. Tags 6-18 are harder to judge, but could also be compared to fitted models. Tag 3 appears too brief to judge, but I don't see any residency so far.

In my mind the classical analysis would be to report an average home-range size (from resident data) and how often individuals disperse (corresponding to segmentation) and an estimate of dispersal ranges (from non-resident data). In a more nomadic species, you can't necessarily make those distinctions, as the individuals are continually dispersing, and there I would just report the large nomadic ranges.

It may be necessary to model the location error, if it is comparable to the distances traveled between the sampled locations. There is a vignette('error') for this: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

Best,
Chris
